# How to Use Ideogram Character for Consistent AI Mascot Visuals

> **In short:** Ideogram's Character feature, available in Ideogram 4.0, lets you design a mascot once and reuse that image as a reference — so the face, hair, outfit, and proportions stay the same while you prompt for new poses, scenes, and props.

You draw a friendly fox in a denim jacket and you love it. Then you need that same fox on a website banner, in a podcast thumbnail, holding a coffee cup, and waving from a T-shirt. The catch with most AI image tools is that "the same character" never really looks the same twice — the nose shifts, the jacket changes color, the hair gets longer, and suddenly you have three different mascots instead of one.

Ideogram's Character feature is built to fix exactly that. Here's how to use it.

## Before you start
- An **Ideogram account** — sign up on Ideogram's official website. Check Ideogram's official pricing page for the current plans and what is included.
- Access to **Ideogram 4.0**, which is the model version that includes the Character feature, according to Ideogram's announcement.
- Roughly **15–20 minutes** for your first mascot set.
- Optional but helpful: a clear idea of who your mascot is (animal, person, robot?), what they wear, and one scene you'd like to start with.

## Step 1 — Create your mascot's "anchor" image
Open Ideogram and start a new image generation. The prompt box is where you type your description — a "prompt" is just the instruction you give the AI, in plain English. Describe your mascot in detail: species, age, clothing, colors, mood, personality. The more specific you are here, the easier every later step gets. Think of this first image as a photo ID card: it's the look every other image has to match. Generate a few options until one really clicks.
💬 Example: "A cheerful cartoon fox with bright orange fur, a cream-colored belly, and a scruffy denim jacket, big round eyes, a small smile, and tufted ears."
You'll know it worked when you see an image you'd happily use everywhere. If it isn't quite right, rephrase the prompt and try again before moving on — this anchor image matters more than any of the later ones.

## Step 2 — Save the image in a place you'll find
Once you have the look you want, save it. Look for a download or save button on the preview — it's usually near the image, sometimes inside a small **⋯ menu** or under a downward-arrow icon. Name the file something obvious, like `mascot-fox-front.png`, so you can spot it instantly in Step 3. If Ideogram has a favorites or gallery feature for your account, adding it there is also a good move.
If you can't find a download button, try opening the image full-size first — many apps hide the save option behind a tap or click on the preview itself.
You'll know it worked when the image sits on your device, named clearly, in a folder you can return to.

## Step 3 — Start a new generation with Character reference
Open a fresh image generation in Ideogram 4.0. Look for an option labeled something like **"Character"**, **"Character reference"**, or an icon of a person next to the prompt box. It may be a button, a tab, or a small upload area — interface names can change, so trust the shape more than the label. When you find it, upload or attach the mascot image you saved in Step 2. The interface should now show your reference image as a small thumbnail near the prompt box, so you can confirm it's the right one.
If you don't see a Character option anywhere, double-check that **Ideogram 4.0** is the model you've selected — earlier versions may not include this feature.
You'll know it worked when the uploaded mascot appears as a thumbnail next to the prompt area, ready to guide the next image.

## Step 4 — Prompt only for what changes
Now describe only the new pose, scene, lighting, or prop — not the mascot itself. The Character reference already "knows" the face, hair, outfit, and proportions, so re-describing them can actually confuse the model and undo the consistency you're trying to build. Keep your prompt focused on what's different this time around.
💬 Example: "Standing and waving at the camera, sunny outdoor background, soft studio lighting, wide banner composition."
You'll know it worked when the new image clearly shows the same fox — same fur, same jacket, same face — but in the new scene you asked for. If it does, you've just created your first consistent variation.

## Step 5 — Build and curate your mascot set
Repeat Steps 3 and 4 for every new scene you need: a T-shirt print, a holiday card, a hero image, a profile photo. Save each result as you go and group them in a folder named after your mascot. If a result drifts — say the jacket turns blue or the ears get pointier — regenerate with a slightly more specific prompt, or swap in a closer reference image from your existing set. After three or four images, your mascot starts to feel like a real character with a life, not just one lucky drawing.
This step is also where consistency starts paying off: you can now place two of your generated images side by side and a stranger would say, "Same character, right?"
You'll know it worked when you have a small library of images that all look like the same character in different moments.

## Common mistakes
- **Re-describing the character in every prompt.** Once Character reference is attached, the model already has the look. Adding "orange fox in denim jacket" again can muddy the result. Prompt only for what's different — pose, scene, lighting, props.
- **Choosing a busy first image as your anchor.** If the anchor photo is small, blurry, or at an awkward angle, every later image inherits those problems. Pick a clean, clear, mostly front-facing (or three-quarter) shot as your reference.
- **Forgetting to check the model version.** Character is part of Ideogram 4.0. If the option isn't appearing, the wrong model version is the most common reason — switch back to Ideogram 4.0 and try again.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** If you run a small business, a side project, or a community group, a consistent mascot makes your website, social posts, and merch feel like one coherent brand instead of a string of unrelated drawings.
- **For your business or work:** Marketing teams, course creators, and product teams can build a recognizable character once and reuse it across landing pages, slide decks, thumbnails, and stickers without hiring an illustrator for every new scene.
- **If you're just getting started:** Start simple — one character (one animal, one outfit, one color palette) and three test scenes. You'll learn the workflow faster than trying to design a whole cast on day one.

## Try it now
Open Ideogram 4.0, write a clear and specific prompt for your mascot, and generate your first anchor image. Save it somewhere you can find again — that's the reference you'll reuse for every scene after this.
